venues.n: Caruso, A Belmond Hotel, Amalfi Coast
venues.d: An 11th-century palace on the cliff-edge of Ravello, with an infinity pool that seems to pour into the sea.
A rose-pink 12th-century villa on the Ravello ridge — 'the pink palace', timeless and serene.
A family-owned grande dame among blooming terraces, with a cliff-lift down to a seawater pool.
A dazzling cliffside newcomer of hand-made majolica and private sea terraces — the coast's most talked-about opening.
A 17th-century Dominican monastery on a private headland — hushed, garden-wrapped and utterly serene.
An 11th-century villa built around the Terrace of Infinity — a garden hotel of rare, literary romance.
A cliff-clinging Amalfi hotel with a seawater pool cut into the rock — honest comfort with a real sea view.
Palazzo Avino's fine-dining room high in Ravello — refined cooking with the whole coast spread beneath.
Dinner in the gardens of Villa Cimbrone — starred cooking beside the Terrace of Infinity.
Borgo Santandrea's sea-terrace kitchen — bright, ingredient-led cooking above a private cove.
Hotel Santa Caterina's flowering-terrace dining room, looking straight out to the Amalfi sea.
Starred cooking in the old refectory of a cliff-top monastery — hushed, considered and beautifully sourced.
Southern Italy's first Michelin star, in a 12th-century ducal palace — history you can taste.
A modern, sea-facing kitchen in Amalfi town doing precise, contemporary Campanian plates.

A dramatic sweep of steps rises to a striped Arab-Norman-Byzantine facade that crowns the whole town. Inside rest the relics of Saint Andrew, and the adjoining Cloister of Paradise — a Moorish garden of slender white columns — is one of the coast's most serene corners.

Housed in a cave-like 13th-century paper mill — the oldest in Europe — this small museum shows how Amalfi made the handmade cotton paper that built its medieval trading power. The guided tour, with the old water-wheels still turning, delights curious children and grandparents alike.

A cool, green ravine of streams, waterfalls and giant prehistoric Woodwardia ferns — living fossils — with the ivy-clad ruins of 12th-century ironworks emerging from the vegetation. A gentle three-hour escape from the heat and the crowds, a small entry fee, best with a nature guide.

A 13th-century palace whose terraced gardens so moved Wagner that he set Parsifal's magic garden here. During the summer Ravello Festival, concerts play on a stage cantilevered over the cliff with only sea and sky behind the orchestra — pure theatre for a romantic evening.

From July into September, Ravello — 'the city of music' — stages classical concerts in Villa Rufolo's gardens, the famous stage floating above the Gulf of Salerno. A sunset chamber recital or grand orchestral night here is one of the coast's most memorable indulgences.

venues.n: Villa Cimbrone & the Terrace of Infinity
venues.d: A romantic garden ending in the Terrazza dell'Infinito, a marble-busted belvedere that Gore Vidal called the most beautiful view in the world — the coast falling away 350 metres to the sea below. Go early or late for the light, and for the honeymoon photograph everyone wants.

A sea cave where sunlight filtering through an underwater fissure turns the whole cavern a glowing emerald green, its floor spiked with stalactites and stalagmites. Reached by lift from the coast road or by boat, it is a short, magical stop — an easy wonder for all ages.

A slim fjord slicing into the cliffs, spanned high above by the coast-road bridge and hiding a tiny pebble beach and cluster of old fishermen's houses at its foot. Every summer divers leap from the 30-metre bridge in an international championship; best admired from the water on a boat day.

venues.n: Vietri sul Mare — the Ceramics Town
venues.d: The 'Capital of Ceramics,' where five centuries of hand-painted majolica spill from every workshop in bold Mediterranean colour. Commission a bespoke dinner service or tiles, and see the Solimene factory's extraordinary curved facade and the tiled Villa Comunale.

On terraces cut vertically into the cliff, family farms grow the prized Sfusato Amalfitano lemon — huge, fragrant, PGI-protected. Walk the pergolas, pick your own fruit, distil a bottle of limoncello to take home, and taste lemon cake in the shade; children love the ritual.

Learn to make fresh pasta, seafood or classic Campanian dishes in a hillside kitchen or amid the lemon groves, then eat what you cooked over a long lunch. Hosts happily build a fully vegetarian menu — ideal for multi-generational groups and a warm, hands-on afternoon.

venues.n: Naples — Cappella Sansevero & the Veiled Christ
venues.d: In a small Baroque chapel lies Sammartino's Cristo Velato, a marble Christ draped in a veil so translucent it seems impossible carved from stone — one of the world's great sculptures. A short, spellbinding visit at the heart of the old city; book timed tickets ahead.

The dead-straight ancient street that literally splits old Naples, lined with churches, cloisters and the year-round nativity artisans of Via San Gregorio Armeno. Loud, alive and utterly authentic — the antidote to the coast's polish, best explored on foot with a guide and a pizza stop.

The treasury of everything portable dug from Pompeii and Herculaneum — the great mosaics, bronzes and frescoes, plus the Farnese marbles. Seeing it before or after the ruins makes the whole story click; a private guide keeps it to the highlights for a two-hour visit.

venues.n: Conca dei Marini & Marina di Conca
venues.d: One of the coast's smallest, most exclusive villages, wrapped around a jewel of a cove below whitewashed houses — long a discreet retreat for the international set. Come by boat for the swimming and the seclusion, and taste the local sfogliatella Santa Rosa where it was invented.
Le Sirenuse's open-air bar suspended above Positano — a French 75 at golden hour, and the finest terrace on the coast.
A club carved into the cliff at the end of Positano's beach — the coast's one true late-night dance floor.
